comments.author: @zubirramli334
comments.text: I believe the biggest reason Malaysia and Singapore became wealthier than Indonesia was how they handled independence. The British may have left politically, but economically, business continued almost as usual. Established companies such as Sime Darby and Guthrie kept operating, supported by the same land laws, banking systems, commercial institutions and infrastructure. This continuity gave Malaysia and Singapore a tremendous advantage in attracting new foreign investment, because the system was already functioning and foreign investors had confidence in it. Indonesia, on the other hand, went through a violent struggle for independence, inherited substantial colonial debt obligations to the Dutch, and later nationalized Dutch-owned businesses, disrupting much of its established commercial system. While Malaysia and Singapore built upon what they inherited, Indonesia spent years dealing with political upheaval, economic restructuring and institutional uncertainty. To me, that difference in continuity is central to understanding why their economic development took such different paths.

comments.author: @beautykostofficial
comments.text:
The question “Why Did Malaysia Get Rich But Indonesia Didn’t?” is fundamentally misleading. It overlooks Indonesia's enormous natural wealth, its distinct national identity, and the historical origins of the Malay language.

First, Bahasa Indonesia is not Bahasa Malaysia.

Indonesia uses Bahasa Indonesia as its national language, while Malaysia uses Bahasa Melayu, also commonly referred to as Bahasa Malaysia. They share historical linguistic roots, but they have developed into distinct national standards, with differences in vocabulary, spelling, pronunciation and usage.

More importantly, Malay is not the property of modern Malaysia. The Malay language and civilisation existed centuries before Malaysia was established in 1963.

Second, the Malay roots of Bahasa Indonesia are deeply connected to Sumatra, particularly Riau and the Riau Islands.

The Riau-Lingga Sultanate became one of the major centres of Malay language, literature and scholarship. Raja Ali Haji and other Riau intellectuals helped develop and standardise written Malay during the nineteenth century.

In 1928, Indonesian nationalists adopted Bahasa Indonesia as their language of unity through the Youth Pledge. It was a conscious decision by the people of the Indonesian archipelago to build their own national identity using a language with deep historical roots in their own region.

Therefore, Indonesia did not take its national language from modern Malaysia. Bahasa Indonesia grew from the Malay heritage of the Indonesian archipelago, with Riau playing a particularly important role.

Third, Indonesia's wealth cannot be judged by GDP per capita alone.

Malaysia may have approximately 2.6 times Indonesia's GDP per capita, but Indonesia's total economy is more than three times larger.

Look at Indonesia's extraordinary natural wealth:

Nickel, copper, gold and other strategic minerals.

Coal, oil and natural gas.

Palm oil, rubber, coffee, cocoa and other agricultural commodities.

Vast forests, fisheries and marine resources.

Enormous land, biodiversity and renewable energy potential.

Indonesia is one of the world's most important resource-producing nations. Its nickel reserves and production alone give it a strategic position in the global electric-vehicle and battery industries.

GDP per capita measures average economic output per person. It does not represent the total value of a nation's natural resources, land, forests, mineral reserves or other national assets.

The real issue is not whether Indonesia has wealth. Indonesia clearly has immense wealth. The challenge is how effectively that wealth is managed, developed through domestic industries and distributed to its people.

Never confuse a higher GDP per capita with greater total national wealth. Malaysia and Indonesia have different economic structures and histories. replies.author: @zubirramli334
replies.text: Actually, GDP per capita adjusted for Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) is a more meaningful measure when comparing average living standards between countries, because it accounts for differences in local prices and purchasing power. According to IMF estimates for 2026, Malaysia's nominal GDP per capita is approximately US$15,981 compared with Indonesia's US$5,153, making Malaysia 3.1 times higher. However, when adjusted for PPP, Malaysia stands at approximately US$47,453 compared with Indonesia's US$19,091, a difference of about 2.5 times. This is a fairer comparison because the cost of living in Indonesia is generally lower. Either way, Malaysia's economic output per person is substantially higher. Of course, GDP per capita does not directly measure household income, wealth distribution or individual well-being, but PPP provides a better basis for comparing average domestic purchasing power.

1. On 1913: Of course Malaysia and Indonesia did not exist as independent nations in 1913. However, economic historians routinely use present-day country names when comparing historical GDP. The Maddison Project does exactly this, reconstructing economic data for territories long before they became independent countries. By your logic, we couldn't discuss India's GDP under British colonial rule either.

2. On language: Bahasa Indonesia developed from Malay, and modern Indonesian and Malaysian Malay share the same linguistic roots. They are closely related and largely mutually intelligible. Nobody is claiming that Javanese and Malay are the same language, or that every Indonesian is ethnically Malay. Also, ethnic Malays are not confined to Peninsular Malaysia and a tiny part of Sumatra. Significant Malay communities exist across Sumatra, the Riau Islands and Borneo. You're confusing ethnicity, nationality and language.

3. On leaving after one minute: That's entirely your choice. But dismissing an entire video after watching just one minute, while making confidently incorrect claims about historical economic comparisons and linguistics, doesn't exactly strengthen your criticism.

Constructive criticism is always welcome, but it helps to get the facts right first.

1. The video says “British Malaya”, not Malaysia. Comparing territories before they became countries is standard in economic history: the Maddison Project puts the Dutch East Indies at $1,361 per person in 1913 vs $1,289 for British Malaya. Also, Malaya became independent in 1957 and Malaysia was formed in 1963, not “after 1945”.

2. Malay is a language, not only an ethnicity. Bahasa Indonesia is a standardised form of Malay, and standard Malaysian and Indonesian are largely mutually intelligible. Nobody said Javanese is Malay: most Indonesians speak Javanese, Sundanese and others at home, and almost all of them also speak Indonesian.
